agent_trace.summary: On abdominal and pelvic CT, a large hypodense mass is often assessed by its relationship to nearby organs, retroperitoneal structures, mesentery, and vascular landmarks such as the iliac vessels and abdominal aorta. Determining the site of origin requires following the mass to the organ or tissue it appears continuous with, while noting displacement versus invasion of adjacent bowel loops, fat planes, and bones.

key_facts: A hypodense mass on CT usually appears darker than surrounding soft tissue because it contains fluid, fat, necrosis, or less cellular material.
The structure of origin is identified by continuity of the lesion with an organ, mesentery, retroperitoneum, or abdominal wall.
In the abdomen/pelvis, important landmarks include bowel loops, mesenteric fat, iliac vessels, lower lumbar vertebrae, and pelvic organs.
Mass effect can displace nearby bowel or vessels without necessarily arising from them.
Loss of fat planes or direct extension may suggest the mass is arising from or invading a nearby structure.
